claim: A test file's processor seconds rise with the core count of the machine it runs on, and the audit Job's CPU limit does not hold them down, because that limit never reaches the compiler. The TypeScript 7 compiler is Go, and Go sets GOMAXPROCS from the cgroup the process is in rather than from any ancestor of it. Akasha's runner moves every test file and every check into a cgroup of its own to meter it, and writes no cpu.max there, so the Job's limit of 8 is invisible and the compiler spins one worker per core of the node it landed on. The audit lands on nodes of 8, 12, 12 and 32 cores, so on the largest that is four times the limit. Those workers buy no clock on a small program and spend processor seconds against the very ceiling the file is judged by. Whoever reads a cost row, sets a ceiling, or tunes a file under one is reading a number that holds only for the node it was taken on.

evidence:
Measured on 2026-09-19. The workstation is 24 cores and runs agents under no CPU quota. The audit runs as a cluster Job, dispatched by check/modules/audit-job, whose spec states requests cpu 2 and limits cpu 8 at infrastructure/job/modules/cluster-running/cluster-running.module.code.ts and names no GOMAXPROCS. Its node selector admits node-01 at 8 cores, node-04 at 12, node-05 at 12 and node-06 at 32.

What one compiler program build costs, judged through refusalsOver over a staged root holding one small file, with only GOMAXPROCS differing. Processor seconds are the run's own plus its reaped children, from fields 14 to 17 of /proc/self/stat, as the mean of ten builds after one warm build. 1: 0.078 processor seconds, 96 ms clock. 2: 0.077, 41 ms. 4: 0.076, 37 ms. 8: 0.086, 37 ms. 16: 0.093, 37 ms. 24: 0.092, 37 ms. The clock stops falling at four and the processor seconds keep rising, so every core past four is spend that buys nothing.

tsgo is built with go1.26.4 and carries no DefaultGODEBUG, so Go's container-aware GOMAXPROCS is on, and it works: in a scope whose cpu.max reads 800000 100000 the binary reports gomaxprocs=8 under GODEBUG=schedtrace. What it does not do is consult an ancestor. Moved into a child cgroup of that same scope carrying no cpu.max of its own, the same binary reports gomaxprocs=24.

That child is the shape akasha makes. budgetAt in code/spawning/modules/running/running.module.code.ts walks up for an ancestor whose cgroup.subtree_control already holds cpu and memory, makes akasha-<pid>-<nanos>/run under it, writes memory.high there and reads cpu.stat there. It writes no cpu.max.

Confirmed in the cluster on node-06, on the cluster/ci image, in a pod shaped like the audit Job. nproc reads 32. The container cgroup and the pod cgroup above it both read cpu.max 800000 100000. The pod cgroup holds cpu and memory in subtree_control and is writable, so it is the ancestor budgetAt would pick. tsgo run in the container cgroup reports gomaxprocs=8. tsgo moved into a child made under the pod cgroup, as akasha would make it, reports gomaxprocs=32, while the pod's 8-CPU quota still binds what it may spend.

What that costs, on the workstation under an 800 percent quota, for one build: 0.082 processor seconds in the quota's own cgroup at gomaxprocs 8, against 0.091 in a child of it at gomaxprocs 24, for the same 36 ms of clock. An eighth of the spend bought nothing.

What this does not yet account for: the typecheck audit's own cost rows hold 33 runs between 2026-09-18 and 2026-09-19, and 32 of them sit between 69.09 and 84.82 child processor seconds with a single outlier at 150.25. There is no four-way clustering matching the four node sizes, so the mechanism is measured but its share of what the audit actually spends is not. Those rows record no node, so no run can be tied to the node it ran on.

The ceiling this bears on is maxCpuSeconds 5 at code/module/properties/test.code-file-property.ts, compared in beyondIn at code/running/modules/code-tests/code-tests.module.code.ts against the cgroup total for the bun test process and every descendant, so the compiler's workers are charged to the file.

Two ways to close it, neither landed here: state GOMAXPROCS in the audit Job's environment, which reaches that Job alone, or have the runner copy the effective cpu.max into the cgroup it makes, which reaches every Go program akasha meters anywhere. infrastructure/job owns the first and code/spawning the second.

Neighbouring ground, each a test file's processor seconds moving for a reason that is not the test's work: a-test-file-pays-the-memory-ceilings-reclaim-as-its-own-processor-time, where a memory ceiling charges reclaim to the file, and a-checks-ceiling-fires-on-a-busy-machine-rather-than-on-a-check-that-slowed, where load on one machine inflates a check. This one differs in the limit meant to hold the spend down being the thing that hides itself from the program doing the spending.
